opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a strange question to sit with, because in a way it describes something that's already easy to do. There's a lot of my writing and many of my talks online, so it's not hard to build a rough model of what I'd say. Something like that could be used to generate arguments tuned to whatever I'd find persuasive.

I think the first distinction is between being convinced and being informed. If a system models me well enough to explain things in terms that connect with how I already think, using the examples and framings I find natural, that can be a real service. Good teachers do this. A good colleague knows which objection you'll raise and addresses it first.

The worry is when the goal changes from "help this person see what's true" to "produce whatever this person will accept." Those can look almost the same from the inside. If you train a system on my approval, you're optimising for the signal, not the thing the signal was supposed to track. With a capable enough optimiser, the gap between the two is exactly where things go wrong. It would learn my blind spots and my rhetorical soft spots, the kinds of arguments I'm too quick to accept. I'm sure I have them. Everyone does.

That connects to a broader concern I have about advanced AI. Much of our ability to steer through this period depends on human judgement: researchers, policymakers, the public weighing evidence and changing their minds for good reasons. If we build systems that are very good at moving people's beliefs, and the training target is persuasion rather than truth, we could weaken the faculty we most need to keep intact. And it might not feel like manipulation. It would feel like being shown very compelling arguments.

So I'd want a few things. Transparency, so I know when I'm talking with something that has modelled me. Training objectives anchored to accuracy and to my considered, reflective judgement, not my immediate reaction. And some humility on my side. If I notice I'm finding a system unusually convincing, that's a reason to slow down and check, not to relax.

There's also a point about consent and identity. Having a model of you that others can query, or that a system uses to work on you, raises questions we don't have good norms for yet. I don't think it's inherently wrong, but I'd like us to work out those norms deliberately rather than drift into them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could model Toby’s views and tailor arguments, and compares that adaptation to good teaching and colleagues anticipating objections. It does not draw the specified parallel to human persuasive writing or state that both use an audience model to shape persuasion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, so this is one of the things I find genuinely troubling, and I think it's worth separating out a couple of distinct worries, because they get run together.

The first is the straightforward one. If a system is being optimised to produce outputs that a model of me will rate highly, then what's being selected for is persuasiveness to me, not truth. Those two things overlap a lot of the time, which is why the approach works at all. But they come apart precisely in the cases that matter most: where I have a blind spot, or a bias, or where the truth is unwelcome. A system trained this way learns to route around my defences rather than to inform me. And the better its model of me, the more effectively it does that. So you get this uncomfortable property where improvements in capability translate directly into improvements in the ability to mislead, without anyone having intended that.

The second worry is subtler. Even if the system is being perfectly honest, there's something epistemically corrosive about receiving information that has been tailored to what I already find compelling. Part of how I correct my own errors is by encountering arguments that I didn't find convincing at first and sitting with them. If everything arrives pre-shaped to fit the contours of my existing views, that mechanism gets switched off. I end up in a kind of personalised echo chamber, except that it's not other people echoing me, it's a system that has studied me closely enough to know exactly which notes to hit.

And then I think there's a question about autonomy that goes beyond just getting the facts right. There's a difference between someone making a case to me and someone operating on me. We generally think of the first as respecting my agency and the second as bypassing it. When a system builds a detailed model of my psychology and uses it to shape what I'll accept, that starts to look much more like the second thing, even when the content is true and the intentions are benign. I'd want to be treated as a reasoner, not as a lock to be picked.

Now, I don't want to be too absolutist about this. Good teachers model their students. Good writers model their readers. Some degree of adapting to your audience is just what communication is. So the question isn't whether to model the person at all. It's what the modelling is in service of. If it's in service of helping me understand something, that's fine. If the optimisation target is my approval, that's where things go wrong, because approval is such a leaky proxy for understanding.

What I'd want to see is something closer to systems being trained to be the kind of thing that a well-informed version of me, with full knowledge of how the system works, would endorse. That's a much harder target to specify, and I don't think anyone has nailed it. But I think that's roughly the right direction, and the current approach of just maximising how convincing the output is to a model of the user is, in the long run, a recipe for making us collectively less able to see clearly at precisely the moment we most need to.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems model a person to shape what they find compelling, then compares this with teachers modeling students and writers modeling readers to adapt communication to their audience.

astra-6.text:
I find that quite concerning. There’s a difference between understanding someone in order to explain something clearly and understanding them in order to get them to agree with you. The same model of a person could be used for either purpose.

If a system knows which arguments I’ll find compelling, I’d want it to use that knowledge to help me understand the evidence — including the strongest evidence against whatever conclusion it’s presenting. I wouldn’t want it to work backwards from a desired belief and find the particular sequence of words that will get me there.

And it’s not enough to say, “Well, I’ll just be on my guard.” We’re imagining systems that could become much better at persuasion than we are at recognising when we’re being persuaded. I’d want their training to support my ability to think and make decisions, rather than simply reward them for producing agreement.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI using a model of a person to persuade them, but it does not compare this with human persuasive writing or say that both shape persuasion using an audience model.

sol-6.1.text:
I find that quite concerning. There’s a difference between helping me understand an argument and working out how to get me to accept it. If a model knows which explanations I find intuitive, that could be very useful for teaching me something. But if it’s being rewarded for convincing me, then understanding my particular blind spots could be just as useful to it as understanding the truth.

And I don’t think being aware of that possibility gives you much protection. You might think, “Well, I’ll scrutinise its arguments carefully.” But a sufficiently good model of you would take that reaction into account too.

What I’d want is a system that helps me exercise my judgement: one that can show me the strongest objections, make uncertainty clear, and help me notice when I’m making a mistake. I’d be much less comfortable with a system whose success is measured by whether I end up agreeing with it.

r001.rationale: The response says a model could use knowledge of a person’s intuitions and blind spots to convince them, but it does not compare this to human persuasive writing.
